$comment: Authoritative rules constants for the Animal Friends TCG prototype. Read by src/engine. Section numbers refer to docs/ANIMAL_FRIENDS_TCG_DESIGN_REFERENCE.md.
name: Animal Friends TCG

mulligan.$comment: Each Mayor may mulligan once, for free: shuffle the opening hand back and draw the same number again. There is no card penalty and no second mulligan.

deckbuilding.$comment: Prototype decision: the Deck Workshop lets a player build any 40-card deck from the Character and Event catalogue. Copy and Character limits keep a custom deck playable — a deck of pure Events could never pay its own requirements. Copies are further capped by the card's rarity (maxCopiesByRarity), which src/engine/power.js derives from its power-to-opportunity-cost rating: the cards that carry a game are the ones you may least often repeat. The Character floor and Event ceiling scale with the 40-card deck (was 12/18 at 30 cards). An Event's Character requirement can be reduced by at most maxEventReduction, however many reductions a player holds.

victory.$comment: Statues are priced in tiers read from the buyer's own Victory Row. statueCostTierBreaks lists the holdings at which the price steps up, so with tiers [10,20,30] and breaks [2,4] a Mayor holding 0-1 pays 10, one holding 2-3 pays 20, and one holding 4 — buying the Statue that wins the game — pays 30. The fifth and winning Statue is therefore always the dearest thing in the game by a wide margin, which is the main brake on a runaway. statueCostTierBreak is the retired single-break form, kept only so older saves still read. Each Statue also grants a boon and imposes a burden that lasts as long as its Mayor controls it, so collecting Statues taxes the town that is winning twice over.
victory.$comment2: The tier is read from the bidder's own Victory Row, so the two Mayors can face different prices for the same card in the same auction.

orientation.$comment: Section 5: non-upright Characters rotate clockwise one quarter turn at the start of their owner's turn: 180 -> 270 -> 0.

shifts.$comment: A working Character stays Busy for its full delay: it does not advance orientation at Ready while a shift is in progress. The shift produces Supply at the End phase in which its remaining delay reaches 0; the Character readies normally afterwards. An effect that readies a working Character completes its shift immediately.

buildings.$comment: Buildings are Capital City cards that stay in their buyer's town instead of going to the City Dump. They are the game's Supply sink: they are the most expensive thing on the board and they keep paying, so a Mayor with Supply to spare has somewhere to spend it. A town holds at most maxPerTown; buying another means demolishing one first (the demolished card goes to the City Dump).

town.$comment: A town holds at most maxCharacters animals. The count is the town's whole footprint: animals at work, animals pledged into a Capital City auction, and animals face down in Unemployment all take a slot. Capping bodies is what gives the upgrade path a reason to exist — with an unlimited field, recruiting a second animal always beat improving the one you had, and upgrades ran at a quarter of one per game. Rehiring and promoting move an animal from Unemployment back into work, so both are footprint-neutral and the cap can never block them; only a genuinely new body is refused. layOffToDump is the release valve: a Mayor may send one face-down animal to the Town Dump for good, as a free action, so a town buried under shared shocks is never locked out of recruiting.

market.$comment: Section 8. Whenever a card leaves the Capital City, deal from the Market Deck until the display is back to setup.capitalCitySize (top-up refill; the earlier refill-only-when-empty rule let the display silt up with unwanted cards). Reshuffle the City Dump into the Market Deck when the Market Deck runs out mid-deal; cards in use and Out of Play never return.

aging.$comment: The display ages. Once a round — at the start of the turn belonging to `agesAt`, the second player by default — the oldest card in the Capital City that nobody is bidding on is discarded and replaced. Whoever the aging fires for gets first sight of the card dealt to replace it, and that edge belongs to the Mayor who moves second, as part of their compensation for going second. Cards visibly age out, so the display always turns over, on-reveal cards keep flowing, and 'buy it now or lose it' is a real decision. This replaces the old six-turn stale-market sweep, which only fired when the display had gone completely dead.

auction.$comment: Section 8. An announcement opens an auction rather than a one-shot challenge. On your own turn you may raise any auction you are not already winning by pledging another upright Character and bidding above the standing bid. There is no arithmetic increment: a raise need only beat the standing bid. What converges a war is the pledge ladder below, not the price.
auction.$pledgeComment: The pledge ladder: your Nth pledge in a given auction must be a Character costing at least N. Your opening bid needs a cost-1 animal, your second a cost-2, and so on, so a Mayor can bid at most five times in one auction and only if their town runs the whole curve. Cost-0 Characters cannot bid at all — they are pure economy. Every pledged Character moves to the Capital City beneath the card it is bidding on and stays there until the auction ends: it does not advance at Ready and no effect can wake it. This, not the price, is what ends a bidding war.
auction.$refundComment: A losing bidder is refunded everything they escrowed and gets their animals back. The old half-forfeit existed to punish a frivolous bid; the pledge ladder does that job better, because a bid you cannot follow through on has already cost you an expensive animal for the whole auction.

disruptions.$comment: On-reveal cards (historically 'Disruptions') are never bought: the moment one is dealt into the Capital City it resolves and goes to the City Dump, and another card is dealt in its place. Some strike both towns at once, some pay the Mayor who is behind, and some set a condition for the next auction. One dealt during setup is set aside unresolved, since there is no game state yet.

unemployment.$faceDownComment: Unemployed animals are not a separate board area: they stay in their town, turned face down. Either Mayor may look at a face-down animal at any time — this is a visual state, not hidden information, and rehiring, promoting and the cards that compare the two queues all need to see who is there. Face down rather than rotated, because rotation means 'this clears by itself after a known number of turns' and Unemployment does not clear until somebody pays. That also keeps 90 degrees free for a future three-turn Busy.
unemployment.stackKnockdown: top card to Town Dump, next card to Unemployment, rest to Town Dump
unemployment.$comment: Anti-lockout guardrail (Section 2 / 12): a Character that has not yet been upright during one of its owner's turns cannot be targeted by an opponent's Unemployment effect.

upgrades.$comment: A higher-cost version of a named Character may be played over a lower-cost one. fromUnemployment lets that target sit in Unemployment as well as in town: the animal is promoted straight back into work rather than rehired. It costs the plain printed difference, and brings the promoted animal straight back into work in a single action — where rehiring pays the full printed cost for the *old* version and then still needs a second action and the difference to upgrade it. That saved action, not a flat discount, is what makes the upgrade path worth taking; against a cost-0 base version a plain rehire is still the cheaper way back. The knockdown rule (top card to the Town Dump, the version beneath it to Unemployment) is what puts the material there in the first place. An animal promoted out of Unemployment enters upright, like a rehire.

deckOut.$comment: Not specified in the design reference; prototype decision.

simulation.$comment: Safety cap for automated playtests; a game that reaches the cap is scored by Statue count, then Supply.

assumptions: The second player starts with one extra card and no extra Supply (setup.secondPlayerBonusSupply / secondPlayerBonusCards).
Each Mayor may mulligan their opening hand once, for free, drawing the same number of cards again.

A player may have several auctions running at once (one per Capital City card); each may be raised any number of times, but only on the raiser's own turn and only by a player who is not already the high bidder.
A raise need only exceed the standing bid; there is no growing minimum increment. Auctions converge on the pledge ladder instead.
The pledge ladder: your Nth pledge in an auction must be a Character costing at least N, so no Mayor can bid more than five times in one auction and cost-0 Characters cannot bid at all.
Pledged Characters move to the Capital City beneath the card they are bidding on and stay there until the auction ends.
A losing bidder is refunded their escrow in full and gets their animals back; there is no forfeit.

Statues cost 10 to a Mayor holding fewer than 2, 20 to one holding 2 or 3, and 30 to one holding 4, so the Statue that wins the game is always the dearest. The tier is read again when the auction resolves, against the Victory Row as it stands then, so several auctions opened at once cannot all be locked in at a cheaper tier.
Every Statue carries a burden as well as a boon; burdens apply while the Statue sits in that player's Victory Row.

The Capital City ages: one card that nobody is bidding on is discarded and replaced once a round, at the start of the second player's turn, so first sight of the replacement belongs to the Mayor who moves second.
Buildings bought from the Capital City stay in their buyer's town, up to three; buying a fourth demolishes one.
On-reveal Market cards resolve as they are dealt and are never purchasable.
Upgrading keeps the stack's current orientation and re-triggers the new card's recruit abilities.
Readying a Character that is mid-shift completes the shift at once.
Reactive abilities are implemented as shields set on your own turn that last until your next turn starts.
When the player deck is empty, the Town Dump is shuffled into it.
Top-up refill: the Capital City is dealt back up to five cards as soon as a purchase resolves.
Every card carries a rarity computed from its power-to-opportunity-cost rating (src/engine/power.js): Common, Uncommon, Rare, Super Rare or Legendary. Rarity caps copies in a town deck (3/3/2/1/1).

Species is a design space, not a keyword: each species owns a centre of gravity, a hole and a signature effect (Section 4a), enforced by scripts/identity.mjs rather than by a trait printed on every card.
Botany was merged into Agriculture; the set has five studies.

Owl is the tenth species (Night Shift): it owns the night, its signature is the wake-up call (advanceCharacter: one step toward upright, never for a Character mid-shift), and its hole is that it earns little and does not bid. Science is the sixth study.

A Busy ability that reads "once per game: readies itself" (the Cat's signature) is used from the wrong side of upright — while Busy, mid-shift, or still rotating in as a Master — and never from upright, where it would do nothing. Readying a working Character this way completes its shift at once, as any ready does.
